ev.jpn_h_genpei.title: The Taira–Minamoto war
ev.jpn_h_genpei.text: The houses of Taira and Minamoto are at war. Armies under red and white banners pass through your lands, taking rice and dragging people off to carry loads. The grown-ups speak in whispers and hide grain in pits — something you will remember all your life.
ev.jpn_h_genpei.note: The Genpei War (1180–1185) began with Prince Mochihito's call to rise against the all-powerful Taira no Kiyomori. It was won by the Minamoto under Yoritomo, and its outcome was the first warrior government — the shogunate at Kamakura.
ev.jpn_h_nara_burn.title: Nara in flames
ev.jpn_h_nara_burn.text: The grown-ups often told you about that winter afterwards: the Taira armies burned the temples of Nara — Tōdaiji with its Great Buddha, and Kōfukuji. Many who sought refuge in the halls died. No one remembered such sacrilege.
ev.jpn_h_nara_burn.note: In the last days of 1180 by the old calendar (January 1181), Taira no Shigehira burned Tōdaiji and Kōfukuji in Nara, which had sided with the Taira's enemies. Rebuilding Tōdaiji became a cause for the whole country.
ev.jpn_h_yowa.title: The Yōwa famine
ev.jpn_h_yowa.text: Drought, crop failure, and then pestilence — the Yōwa famine. In the capital the dead lie in the streets, and monks write a sacred letter on their foreheads so the souls can find their way. You are fed thin gruel from the last of the stores.
ev.jpn_h_yowa.note: The Yōwa famine (1181–1182) struck western Japan, weakening the Taira, who depended on its rice. Kamo no Chōmei wrote in his Hōjōki (1212) that over 42,000 people died in the capital alone.
ev.jpn_h_dannoura.title: Dan-no-ura
ev.jpn_h_dannoura.text: In spring the news came: the Taira fleet was destroyed in the strait at Dan-no-ura. The child emperor Antoku went to the bottom with his grandmother and the sacred sword. You are still small, but you will remember the grown-ups praying for the drowned.
ev.jpn_h_dannoura.note: The naval battle of Dan-no-ura (1185) in the Shimonoseki strait ended the Genpei War. Kiyomori's widow leapt into the sea with the six-year-old Emperor Antoku; one of the three imperial regalia, the sword, was lost.
ev.jpn_h_jito.title: A new steward
ev.jpn_h_jito.text: A new jitō steward has arrived on the estate — a warrior from the east, the shogun's man from Kamakura. He ordered the fields and people to be registered afresh and made it clear at once that he is the one to obey now.
ev.jpn_h_jito.note: In 1185 the court allowed Minamoto no Yoritomo to appoint military governors (shugo) and estate stewards (jitō) throughout the country. This is how warrior power reached every village.
ev.jpn_h_shogun.title: Shogun
ev.jpn_h_shogun.text: Minamoto no Yoritomo has received from the court the title of sei-i taishōgun, "great general who subdues the barbarians". Kamakura celebrates, while at court in Kyoto lips are pursed: the country is now ruled by warriors.
ev.jpn_h_shogun.note: In 1192 Yoritomo was appointed sei-i taishōgun. The Kamakura shogunate (1185/1192–1333) was Japan's first warrior government; the emperor and court remained in Kyoto.
ev.jpn_h_jokyu.title: The Jōkyū War
ev.jpn_h_jokyu.text: The retired emperor Go-Toba has called on the whole country to rise against the Hōjō regents. Kamakura has answered with an army that is already marching on the capital, and everyone has to pick a side.
ev.jpn_h_jokyu.court.success: The court lost, but you were left alone — too small a fish to matter.
ev.jpn_h_jokyu.court.failure: After Kamakura's victory the lands of the court's supporters were confiscated. Yours too.
ev.jpn_h_jokyu.kamakura.success: The victors are handing out confiscated lands. Something came your way too.
ev.jpn_h_jokyu.kamakura.failure: You were wounded in the fighting at the Uji river.
ev.jpn_h_jokyu.note: The Jōkyū War (1221): Go-Toba tried to overthrow the Hōjō regents, but Kamakura's army took Kyoto within a month. Three retired emperors were exiled, over 3,000 estates of the court's supporters were confiscated, and the Rokuhara deputyship was set up in Kyoto.
ev.jpn_h_kanki.title: The Kanki famine
ev.jpn_h_kanki.text: A cold summer, snow in July, then drought — the great Kanki famine. People eat grass and bark, and the dead lie by the roads. For the time being the shogunate has allowed people to sell themselves into service to anyone with rice, just to survive.
ev.jpn_h_kanki.share: Share your last with the neighbours
ev.jpn_h_kanki.own: Keep your stores for your own
ev.jpn_h_kanki.sell: Sell yourself into service to a rich house
ev.jpn_h_kanki.note: The Kanki famine (1230–1232) was one of the worst in medieval Japan, killing a significant share of the population. The shogunate temporarily permitted the sale of people into bondage and later tried to restore their freedom.
ev.jpn_h_goseibai.title: A law code for warriors
ev.jpn_h_goseibai.text: The regent Hōjō Yasutoki has proclaimed the Goseibai Shikimoku, a code of 51 articles: how to divide land and inheritance, how to judge disputes between warriors and estates. Scribes copy it out, and those who can read recite it aloud in the squares.
ev.jpn_h_goseibai.note: The Goseibai Shikimoku (1232) was the first law code of the warrior class. Based on warrior custom and Kamakura's court practice, it remained in force, with additions, for several centuries.
ev.jpn_h_shoka.title: The Shōka disasters
ev.jpn_h_shoka.text: First a great earthquake in Kamakura, then a cold summer, famine and pestilence. The monk Nichiren writes to the regent that it is all punishment for false teachings. People don't know whom to believe.
ev.jpn_h_shoka.help: Help the monks feed the hungry
ev.jpn_h_shoka.note: The Shōka years (1257–1260) brought an earthquake in Kamakura (1257), crop failures, famine and epidemics. In 1260 Nichiren presented the regent with his treatise "On Establishing the Correct Teaching for the Peace of the Land", blaming the calamities on abandoning the Lotus Sutra.
ev.jpn_h_bunei.title: Mongols at Hakata
ev.jpn_h_bunei.text: In autumn a fleet of Mongols and Koreans anchored off Hakata — hundreds of ships. Landing to the beat of drums and gongs, they shoot poisoned arrows and hurl exploding shells. The samurai fall back, and Hakata is burning.
ev.jpn_h_bunei.fight: Stand with the samurai on the shore
ev.jpn_h_bunei.fight.success: You held until evening. By morning the bay was empty: the enemy had gone, and they say a storm wrecked part of the fleet.
ev.jpn_h_bunei.fight.failure: A poisoned arrow struck your thigh. You lived, but could not walk for a long time.
ev.jpn_h_bunei.temple: Take refuge in a temple and pray
ev.jpn_h_bunei.temple.success: The enemy left the temple alone. By morning the bay was empty.
ev.jpn_h_bunei.temple.failure: The fire reached the temple too. You got out burned and with nothing.
ev.jpn_h_bunei.note: The first Mongol invasion (Bun'ei, 1274): Kublai's forces from Korea took Tsushima and Iki and landed at Hakata. After a day's fighting the fleet withdrew, part of it lost in a storm. The samurai were stunned by unfamiliar tactics, poison and gunpowder bombs.
ev.jpn_h_bourui.title: The stone wall
ev.jpn_h_bourui.text: The shogunate has ordered a stone wall taller than a man built along Hakata Bay in case the Mongols land again. Every estate on Kyushu must provide men and stone, section by section.
ev.jpn_h_bourui.pay: Pay for a labourer in your place
ev.jpn_h_bourui.evade.success: The headman looked the other way, and you were forgotten.
ev.jpn_h_bourui.evade.failure: You were listed among the shirkers: a fine and sidelong looks from the neighbours.
ev.jpn_h_bourui.note: In 1276 a stone defensive wall (genkō bōrui) 2–3 m high was built along some 20 km of Hakata Bay by the vassals and estates of Kyushu. Remains of the wall survive to this day.
ev.jpn_h_koan.title: The divine wind
ev.jpn_h_koan.text: The Mongols have come back — twice as many, from Korea and from southern China. But the wall holds, and at night the samurai raid the ships from light boats. In early autumn a terrible typhoon strikes and smashes the enemy fleet. People say the kami sent a divine wind — kamikaze.
ev.jpn_h_koan.note: The second invasion (Kōan, 1281) was the largest naval expedition of its time. The wall kept the Mongols from landing at Hakata; after nearly two months of fighting a typhoon destroyed most of the fleet. The victory was credited to the temples and shrines that had prayed for the country's protection.
ev.jpn_h_einin_quake.title: Earthquake in Kamakura
ev.jpn_h_einin_quake.text: At dawn an earthquake shook Kamakura. Temples and houses collapsed and fires broke out; they say thousands died. And a few days later, in the confusion, the regent destroyed his all-powerful adviser Taira no Yoritsuna.
ev.jpn_h_einin_quake.dig.success: You pulled a neighbouring family out from under the debris. They will pray for you as long as they live.
ev.jpn_h_einin_quake.dig.failure: A falling beam pinned you down.
ev.jpn_h_einin_quake.note: The 1293 Kamakura earthquake killed, according to the chronicles, more than 20,000 people. Taking advantage of the chaos, the regent Hōjō Sadatoki destroyed the house of his powerful adviser Taira no Yoritsuna.
ev.jpn_h_tokusei.title: An edict of grace
ev.jpn_h_tokusei.text: The shogunate has issued an "edict of virtuous government": land sold or pawned by the shogun's vassals goes back to its former owners without payment. The moneylenders are furious; ruined warriors rejoice.
ev.jpn_h_tokusei.note: The Einin tokusei (1297) was the shogunate's attempt to rescue vassals ruined by divided inheritance and the costs of the Mongol wars. It undermined confidence in lending and caused discontent; part of it was soon repealed.
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.title: The end of Kamakura
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.text: Nitta Yoshisada's army broke into Kamakura along the shoals by Cape Inamura. The city is burning; the regent Hōjō Takatoki and hundreds of his men have taken their own lives at Tōshōji temple. A century and a half of Kamakura rule ended in a few days.
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.text.kyoto: Ashikaga Takauji, sent by the shogunate against Emperor Go-Daigo, went over to the emperor and took Rokuhara, Kamakura's headquarters in the capital. A few weeks later the news came: Kamakura itself had fallen and the Hōjō regents were dead.
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.defend.success: Your quarter survived, and the victors took no revenge on those who had merely defended their homes.
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.defend.failure: You were wounded and your house was burned.
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.join.success: The victors rewarded those who joined them in time generously.
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.join.failure: You were wounded in street fighting, and others got the rewards.
ev.jpn_h_kamakura_fall.note: In 1333 Emperor Go-Daigo rose against the Hōjō. Ashikaga Takauji seized Rokuhara in Kyoto and Nitta Yoshisada took Kamakura; Hōjō Takatoki killed himself together with hundreds of retainers. The Kamakura shogunate fell.
ev.jpn_h_kenmu.title: The Kenmu Restoration
ev.jpn_h_kenmu.text: Emperor Go-Daigo rules in person — the Kenmu Restoration. But the rewards go to courtiers, and the warriors who shed their blood are left with nothing. On the bank of the Kamo river someone has posted a mocking poem: "What's in fashion in the capital these days: night raids, robbery, forged decrees…"
ev.jpn_h_kenmu.note: The Kenmu Restoration (1333–1336) was Go-Daigo's attempt to restore direct imperial rule. Warrior discontent led to Ashikaga Takauji's revolt. The satirical Nijō-gawara lampoon (1334) mocked the disorder in the capital.
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.title: Two courts
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.text: The country has two emperors: the Northern Court in Kyoto under the Ashikaga, and the Southern Court in the mountains of Yoshino. Bands of one side or the other occupy your lands in turn, demanding rice, men and oaths of loyalty.
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.north.success: The Northern side won out in your region, and you were rewarded for your loyalty.
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.north.failure: Southern raiders struck without warning and ruined your house.
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.south.success: The South's supporters praise your loyalty to the rightful emperor.
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.south.failure: The Northerners fined your house and drove off your livestock.
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.bend: Bow to whoever is stronger at the moment
ev.jpn_h_nanboku.note: The Northern and Southern Courts period (1336–1392): after breaking with Ashikaga Takauji, Go-Daigo fled to Yoshino, and the Ashikaga installed another emperor in Kyoto. The war dragged on for over half a century and ended with the reunification of the courts in 1392.
ev.jpn_h_reunion.title: One emperor
ev.jpn_h_reunion.text: The Southern emperor has returned to the capital and handed the sacred regalia to the Northern Court. Half a century of war between the two courts is over. The temples hold services of thanksgiving, and people can hardly believe it is possible to live without war.
ev.jpn_h_reunion.note: In 1392 the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu brought about the reunification of the courts: the Southern emperor Go-Kameyama handed the regalia to Go-Komatsu. The promise to alternate the throne between the two lines was never kept.
ev.jpn_h_kitayama.title: The Golden Pavilion
ev.jpn_h_kitayama.text: Shogun Yoshimitsu is building a villa in the northern hills of the capital with a pavilion covered in gold leaf. Envoys from China, poets, painters and sarugaku actors gather there — they say the young actor Zeami is high in the shogun's favour.
ev.jpn_h_kitayama.note: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu began building the Kitayama villa with its Golden Pavilion (Kinkakuji) in 1397. His patronage of Kan'ami and Zeami turned sarugaku into the refined Noh theatre.
ev.jpn_h_ming_trade.title: Trade with Ming
ev.jpn_h_ming_trade.text: Shogun Yoshimitsu has accepted from the Ming emperor the title "King of Japan", and tally trade has opened. Swords, copper, sulphur and fans will go to China; silk, books and copper coins will come back. Merchants are looking for partners.
ev.jpn_h_ming_trade.invest.success: The ship came back with silk and coin. Double your money.
ev.jpn_h_ming_trade.invest.failure: The goods got stuck in a Chinese port; the money will be a long time coming back.
ev.jpn_h_ming_trade.stay: Wait and see how it goes
ev.jpn_h_ming_trade.note: In 1401 Yoshimitsu sent an embassy to the Ming, and in 1402 received a reply naming him "King of Japan". The tally (kangō) trade begun in 1404 brought huge profits to the shogunate, temples and the merchants of Hakata and Sakai.
ev.jpn_h_oei.title: Alarm over Tsushima
ev.jpn_h_oei.text: News has come: a Korean fleet has attacked Tsushima, the pirates' lair. Hakata is in a panic — people whisper that the Mongols are back, and merchants hurry to move their goods out of the harbour.
ev.jpn_h_oei.note: The Ōei invasion (1419): Joseon Korea sent a fleet against the wakō bases on Tsushima. At first rumours spread in Japan of a new Mongol invasion.
ev.jpn_h_shocho.title: The Shōchō uprising
ev.jpn_h_shocho.text: Carters from Ōmi have risen, and after them the peasants around the capital: they smash the storehouses of moneylenders and sake brewers, burn the debt notes and demand a tokusei, a cancellation of debts. They say nothing like it has happened since the country was founded.
ev.jpn_h_shocho.join.success: The notes burned right there in the street. Your debt is gone.
ev.jpn_h_shocho.join.failure: The guards broke up the crowd and you were wounded.
ev.jpn_h_shocho.guard: Help the owners defend the storehouses
ev.jpn_h_shocho.guard.success: The storehouse held, and the owner rewarded you generously.
ev.jpn_h_shocho.guard.failure: The crowd swept the guards aside. You took a beating.
ev.jpn_h_shocho.note: The Shōchō uprising (1428) was the first great tokusei ikki: Ōmi carters and Yamashiro peasants sacked moneylenders' storehouses in and around Kyoto. A contemporary wrote that "never since the founding of the country have commoners risen like this".
ev.jpn_h_kansho.title: The Kanshō famine
ev.jpn_h_kansho.text: Drought, locusts, then floods — the Kanshō famine. Refugees from the provinces stream into the capital, the monk Gan'ami cooks gruel for them by the Gojō bridge, and the Kamo river is choked with bodies. Meanwhile Shogun Yoshimasa is rebuilding his palace.
ev.jpn_h_kansho.leave: Go where there are no crowds
ev.jpn_h_kansho.note: The Kanshō famine (1459–1461) was one of the worst in Kyoto's history: records say some 82,000 people died in the capital. Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa carried on with costly building works all the while, drawing reproach even from the emperor.
ev.jpn_h_onin.title: The Ōnin War
ev.jpn_h_onin.text: The houses of Hosokawa and Yamana and their allies have clashed right inside the capital — the Ōnin War has begun. The Eastern and Western camps stand a few blocks apart; temples and palaces burn, and ashigaru mercenaries loot whatever has not yet been burned.
ev.jpn_h_onin.defend.success: Your quarter held: the neighbours built a barricade and keep watch at night.
ev.jpn_h_onin.defend.failure: Your house was burned and you were wounded.
ev.jpn_h_onin.ashigaru: Join the ashigaru — they're fed and paid
ev.jpn_h_onin.note: The Ōnin War (1467–1477) began over the shogunal succession and the leadership of the Hosokawa and Yamana houses. Ten years of fighting turned most of Kyoto into ashes, and the shogun's authority became nominal. The Sengoku period is usually dated from this war.
ev.jpn_h_sakai_rise.title: Ships head for Sakai
ev.jpn_h_sakai_rise.text: While the capital burns, the ships from China come not to Hakata but to Sakai: the Hosokawa route them around their enemies' lands. The harbour is packed, storehouses multiply, and refugees from Kyoto open shops and workshops here.
ev.jpn_h_sakai_rise.note: During the Ōnin War, the Ming trade ships fitted out by the Hosokawa began returning to Sakai (first in 1469). This marked the beginning of Sakai's rise as the country's chief trading port.
ev.jpn_h_hokke.title: The Lotus leagues
ev.jpn_h_hokke.text: Townspeople who follow Nichiren have banded into "Lotus leagues": they armed themselves, burned the Ikkō temple at Yamashina and now run the capital themselves — paying no taxes and holding their own courts. The monks of Mount Hiei threaten them with war.
ev.jpn_h_hokke.join.success: The league is strong, and your quarter has an order it has not seen in years.
ev.jpn_h_hokke.join.failure: The Hiei monks and their allies burned the Nichiren quarters. You barely escaped.
ev.jpn_h_hokke.note: In 1532 the Lotus leagues (Hokke ikki) of Kyoto's townspeople burned the Ikkō sect's Yamashina Honganji and for several years effectively governed the capital. In 1536 Enryakuji and its allies crushed them, burning 21 Nichiren temples and much of lower Kyoto.
ev.jpn_h_teppo.title: Guns
ev.jpn_h_teppo.text: Foreign guns — teppō — have been brought from the southern island of Tanegashima. Smiths are struggling to make the barrel and the breech screw, and lords buy every gun at any price. A gunsmith you know is looking for someone to invest in his workshop.
ev.jpn_h_teppo.invest.success: Orders from lords keep coming. You've tripled your money.
ev.jpn_h_teppo.invest.failure: The barrels burst when tested. The workshop closed and the money was lost.
ev.jpn_h_teppo.note: In 1543 Portuguese travelling on a junk that reached Tanegashima sold the local lord two matchlocks. His smiths copied them, and within a decade Sakai and Kunitomo had become centres of gun production.
ev.jpn_h_xavier.title: A foreign monk
ev.jpn_h_xavier.text: A foreign monk in a shabby black cassock — Francis, they call him — has passed through the town with a baptised Japanese interpreter. He preaches in the streets about an unknown God, and children laugh at him. They say he wants to see the emperor himself.
ev.jpn_h_xavier.text.kyoto: A foreign monk in a shabby cassock, Francis, has come to the war-ravaged capital. He wanted the emperor's permission to preach throughout the country, but he was not admitted, and after a few days he went back west.
ev.jpn_h_xavier.note: The Jesuit Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549, visited Hirado in 1550 and apparently passed through Hakata on his way to Yamaguchi and Kyoto. In early 1551 he spent about eleven days in Kyoto but failed to obtain an audience with the emperor.
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.title: Campaign to Kawanakajima
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.text: The lord of Echigo, Nagao Kagetora, who prays to the war god Bishamonten, is raising an army against Takeda of Kai once again — on the plain of Kawanakajima. Men, horses and rice are being taken from the villages.
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.serve.success: You came back from the campaign in one piece and with a reward.
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.serve.failure: In the morning fog the armies met hand to hand. You were carried off the field wounded.
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.supply: Give rice and a horse to the army
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.hide.success: The collectors passed your house by.
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.hide.failure: They found you in the shed. They took what they wanted anyway, and fined you too.
ev.jpn_h_kawanakajima.note: Nagao Kagetora (from 1561 Uesugi Kenshin) united Echigo and clashed five times (1553–1564) with Takeda Shingen at Kawanakajima. The fourth battle, in 1561, was one of the bloodiest of the Sengoku period.
ev.jpn_h_nobunaga.title: Nobunaga in the capital
ev.jpn_h_nobunaga.text: Oda Nobunaga's army from Owari has entered the capital together with Ashikaga Yoshiaki, whom Nobunaga is making shogun. Surprisingly, his soldiers do not loot: theft is punished with death on the spot.
ev.jpn_h_nobunaga.text.sakai: Oda Nobunaga, who has just taken the capital, has demanded a war levy of twenty thousand strings of coins from Sakai. The city council ordered the moats deepened and rōnin hired, but a year later the city gave in and paid.
ev.jpn_h_nobunaga.note: In 1568 Oda Nobunaga entered Kyoto and installed Ashikaga Yoshiaki as shogun. He demanded 20,000 kan from Sakai; the city first prepared to resist but submitted in 1569.
ev.jpn_h_hiei.title: Mount Hiei in flames
ev.jpn_h_hiei.text: Nobunaga surrounded Mount Hiei and burned the Enryakuji monastery — hundreds of temples, and with them the monks and everyone else who was there. Smoke hung over the mountain for days, and no one in the capital dared speak of it aloud.
ev.jpn_h_hiei.note: In 1571 Oda Nobunaga destroyed Enryakuji, which had sided with his enemies. Estimates of the dead range from 1,500 to 4,000. The monastery's eight-century military and political power was broken.
ev.jpn_h_ishiyama.title: The Ishiyama fortress
ev.jpn_h_ishiyama.text: Nearby, in Osaka, the fortress-temple of Ishiyama Honganji has held out against Nobunaga for ten years. The Ikkō monks and believers pay for powder and rice in silver, and some in Sakai secretly ship them cargo by sea.
ev.jpn_h_ishiyama.honganji.success: The boats slipped past Nobunaga's fleet at night. Huge profit.
ev.jpn_h_ishiyama.honganji.failure: Your boat was intercepted. The cargo was lost, and Nobunaga's men fined you.
ev.jpn_h_ishiyama.neither: Stay out of other people's war
ev.jpn_h_ishiyama.note: The Ishiyama Honganji War (1570–1580) was a ten-year struggle between Oda Nobunaga and the Ikkō sect. The fortress was supplied by sea, including by the Mōri fleet, and surrendered only in 1580 through imperial mediation.
ev.jpn_h_honnoji.title: Honnōji
ev.jpn_h_honnoji.text: Before dawn the general Akechi Mitsuhide surrounded Honnōji temple, where Nobunaga was spending the night. The temple burned, and Nobunaga is no more. Eleven days later Hashiba Hideyoshi, racing back from the west, defeated Akechi at Yamazaki.
ev.jpn_h_honnoji.note: The Honnōji incident (21 June 1582): Akechi Mitsuhide attacked Oda Nobunaga in Kyoto, and Nobunaga took his own life. Hashiba (later Toyotomi) Hideyoshi hurried back from campaign and defeated Akechi at Yamazaki.
ev.jpn_h_kenchi.title: The land survey
ev.jpn_h_kenchi.text: By Hideyoshi's order officials are measuring the fields with a standard rod and recording every plot and who works it. From now on the tax will be taken from these records — without the allowances the old lords used to make.
ev.jpn_h_kenchi.hide.success: The far field never made it into the books.
ev.jpn_h_kenchi.hide.failure: The deception was uncovered. A fine, and shame on the whole village.
ev.jpn_h_kenchi.bribe.success: The surveyor "made a mistake" in your favour.
ev.jpn_h_kenchi.bribe.failure: The surveyor took the gift and wrote it down as it was anyway.
ev.jpn_h_kenchi.note: The Taikō land survey (taikō kenchi, 1582–1598) introduced standard measures and assessed yields in koku of rice. Each plot was registered to a specific farmer, binding him to the land as a taxpayer.
ev.jpn_h_kyushu.title: Hideyoshi on Kyushu
ev.jpn_h_kyushu.text: Hideyoshi has subdued Kyushu with a huge army. Hakata, ravaged by the local lords' wars, is to be rebuilt from scratch with straight streets. And soon an edict was posted on the gates: the Christian padres must leave the country within twenty days.
ev.jpn_h_kyushu.note: In 1587 Toyotomi Hideyoshi forced the Shimazu to submit. He ordered Hakata rebuilt on a new plan (taikō machiwari) and that same year issued an edict expelling missionaries, though at first it was barely enforced.
ev.jpn_h_katanagari.title: The sword hunt
ev.jpn_h_katanagari.text: Hideyoshi's edict: peasants are to hand over their swords, spears, bows and guns. The metal, they say, will be made into nails for the Great Buddha in the capital's temple, and so the peasants will be saved both in this life and the next. Officials are going from house to house.
ev.jpn_h_katanagari.hide: Hide your grandfather's sword under the floor
ev.jpn_h_katanagari.hide.success: The sword stayed in its hiding place. Nobody found it.
ev.jpn_h_katanagari.hide.failure: The sword was found. You had to pay a fine and bow to the headman.
ev.jpn_h_katanagari.note: The sword hunt edict (katanagari) of 1588 disarmed peasants and monks and drew a sharp line between warriors and farmers. Officially the metal was collected for the Buddha statue at Hōkōji temple.
ev.jpn_h_korea.title: The Korean campaign
ev.jpn_h_korea.text: Hideyoshi means to conquer Ming China and has sent armies through Korea. Every village must provide men — soldiers, porters, rowers. Ships leave the harbours of Kyushu one after another, and by no means all come back.
ev.jpn_h_korea.go.success: You came back alive, with a reward and with stories children are better off not hearing.
ev.jpn_h_korea.go.failure: Korean winter, hunger and arrows. You came back, but your health never will.
ev.jpn_h_korea.hide.success: You sat out the levy in the hills, and you were forgotten.
ev.jpn_h_korea.hide.failure: The neighbours gave you away. A fine, and shame on the whole village.
ev.jpn_h_korea.note: Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea (1592–1593 and 1597–1598) cost Korea and Japan itself enormous losses. Troops assembled at Nagoya castle in Hizen; Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet cut the Japanese sea lanes. The armies were recalled after Hideyoshi's death in 1598.
ev.jpn_h_uesugi_move.title: The Uesugi depart
ev.jpn_h_uesugi_move.text: Hideyoshi has moved Lord Uesugi Kagekatsu from Echigo to distant Aizu. Samurai families are loading their belongings and following their lord, while the new lord's people — the Hori — are on their way to take their place.
ev.jpn_h_uesugi_move.note: In 1598 Toyotomi Hideyoshi transferred Uesugi Kagekatsu from Echigo to Aizu with an enlarged domain; Echigo went to Hori Hideharu. The Uesugi retainers left with their lord — this was how Hideyoshi uprooted lords from their power bases.
ev.jpn_h_sekigahara.title: Sekigahara
ev.jpn_h_sekigahara.text: In autumn, in the misty valley of Sekigahara, the Eastern army of Tokugawa Ieyasu met the Western army of the supporters of Hideyoshi's heir. In the middle of the battle some of the Western lords went over to Tokugawa, and it was all decided in a single day.
ev.jpn_h_sekigahara.note: The battle of Sekigahara (21 October 1600) made Tokugawa Ieyasu master of Japan. In 1603 he became shogun; the Tokugawa shogunate ruled until 1868.
